summary:
Most farmers make big decisions on their own. When to water, what to watch out for, what to plant next year. NASA collects data that could help with all of this, but it's hard to find and even harder to read when you're standing in a field.

That's what Basro is for. You mark your field on the map and tell us your crop, when you planted it and how you water. We pull in NASA data on temperature, rainfall, soil moisture and seasonal forecasts, add what you tell us and the photos you take, and give you a simple answer: what to do today and why. The AI helps read photos, but it never makes the call alone. Every suggestion is checked against the data and your field's own history.

Basro is also where farmers meet each other. In BAS Social you can share photos, answer questions, earn XP, move up the rankings in your district, province and country, and find people growing the same crop as you. Everything farmers post adds to the data, so advice gets better in every region where people use it.

Each field keeps its own record from one season to the next, so you can compare with similar fields and plan what to plant next based on what actually worked.

In the long run, we want Basro to become a dataset that follows farmland around the world every day. Farmers build it, farmers use it, and farming gets more efficient.
details:
Basro — Project Details (Team Junglers, NASA Space Apps 2026, Field Shift)

Live demo: https://basro.vercel.app

Source code: https://github.com/kkhjj2/Basro/releases/tag/source-code

What it does

Basro is a farming assistant that lives on the farmer's phone. It answers the questions a farmer actually asks: should I water today, what should I watch out for this week, and what should I plant next on this field. Every answer comes with the reason behind it, the data it used, and what is still unknown.

Field Shift asks for a decision-support tool that uses NASA Earth observations together with local information to help farmers explore crop rotation strategies, while supporting the farmer's judgment instead of replacing it. Basro is built around that idea. NASA data gives the regional picture, the farmer adds what only they know about their own field, and Basro compares the options side by side and says clearly where local knowledge has to confirm the result.

It starts with the field, not with a photo. The farmer picks their field on a world map, then tells us the crop, the previous crop, the planting date, how they water, and what matters most to them. From that moment Basro has a picture of the field it can work with, and everything else is added on top.

Why it matters

Two problems sit behind Basro.

NASA data is hard for farmers to use. A 2023 white paper by the U.S. National Space Council Users' Advisory Group describes Earth observation data as "difficult to use without expert knowledge, expert systems, and often inaccessible to some users." Most of the world's farmers do not have that expertise: about 84% of the world's roughly 570 million farms are smaller than two hectares (Lowder, Skoet and Raney, 2016). Basro does the expert step for them and returns a plain answer.

Farmers decide alone. Advice from someone like you works. In a large field experiment in Malawi, farmers adopted new practices more when the message came from a peer farmer facing similar conditions than from a government extension worker (BenYishay and Mobarak, 2019). Yet digital farming tools are often tried once and not used consistently through the season; a 2024 survey of more than 1,400 Kenyan farmers found adoption "high but inconsistent" (60 Decibels). BAS Social is our answer to both: it connects farmers with neighbors who grow the same crop, and it gives them a reason to come back every day.

How it works:

Take a farmer growing wheat in Doğanşehir, Malatya, Türkiye.

1. Earth data for the field. Basro pulls the area's climate from NASA POWER (temperature, minimum and maximum temperature, rainfall, humidity, surface soil wetness and frost days, with 1991–2020 climate normals) and shows it as map layers and as the field's climate context. It adds a 7-day forecast from Open-Meteo and a monthly seasonal outlook from ECMWF SEAS5. For root-zone soil moisture it uses NASA SMAP L4 (SPL4SMGP, 9 km), retrieved through NASA AppEEARS, as a regional check.

2. A water balance, not a guess. A science engine written in TypeScript follows FAO-56: reference evapotranspiration with the Hargreaves equation, crop water use as ETc = Kc * ET0 with stage-based crop coefficients, and root-zone depletion. The result is a 3D soil block: how much usable water is in the root zone now, after watering, and in 7 days if you don't water.

3. Rotation options, compared side by side. The Crop Rotation Engine compares three next-crop sequences for the field, starting from its current crop, for example one that changes plant family, one that puts water first, and one with a legume and soil cover. In the Rotation Lab, for cereal and pulse fields, it screens every three-year sequence of wheat, barley, chickpea and lentil, including repeating the current crop. It excludes sequences that follow a crop with one from the same plant family, ranks the rest by water, crop diversity and how familiar they are to the farmer, and lets the farmer change those priorities. It then checks each option under drier and warmer conditions. For each option it shows why it fits, which data it used, what the risks are, what is uncertain and which measurement could change the answer. For orchards, such as Malatya's apricots, it keeps the trees and compares ground-cover options instead.

4. The farmer's own data changes the answer. Basro asks for the one missing piece of information most likely to change its advice (for example, how long water stood on the field after rain, or the previous crop) and turns it into a small task. Farmers can also enter soil test results, which feed into the water calculation. When a new answer comes in, Basro recalculates and shows "What changed?" with a before and after.

5. Photos with honest limits. The farmer takes a photo of the plant. A vision model reports the crop, the visible growth stage, whether the photo is usable and how confident it is. If confidence is low, or the crop doesn't match the field, it says so and asks for a new photo instead of guessing.

6. Field memory. Photos, decisions, notes and tasks go into one timeline for the field, and a weekly report sums it up in plain words.

The AI never makes the decision on its own. NASA data and the farmer's own data come first, the science engine does the calculation, and the AI helps read photos and explain the result in plain language. There are things we never take from a photo: soil moisture, irrigation need, a disease diagnosis, or a fertilizer or pesticide dose. Every rotation result says it is not planting approval: local variety, sowing window, disease history, soil test and water budget have to be confirmed on the ground.

BAS Social: why farmers come back, and how the data grows

Most farming apps get opened once and forgotten. BAS Social is what brings farmers in and keeps them coming back every day. Farmers see what their neighbors are posting at district, province, region and country level. They share photos, like and comment, answer one-tap questions about their fields, and compare how much their crop grew this week against others growing the same crop. They earn XP for tasks and posts, keep a daily streak, and level up from Seedling all the way to Veteran. A crop mastery ranking shows where they stand.

It is also Basro's data engine. Every post, answer and photo is new data about real fields, collected by the people who farm them. That is the ground information NASA data cannot see on its own, and it goes back into the system, so the more farmers use Basro, the better its advice gets. A district or province agriculture director sees a summary panel with aggregate numbers only: active farmers, posts, signals from the field and growth by crop.

The seven systems:

- Earth Intelligence: world map with NASA POWER climate layers, weather forecast, seasonal outlook, SMAP soil moisture.

- AI Intelligence: photo review that abstains when unsure, weekly report, farming assistant chat.

- Farm Memory: a timeline of each field's photos, decisions and notes.

- Farm Twins: with the farmer's consent, compares the field with similar fields (same crop, same climate zone, close growth stage) to learn from shared experience.

- Ground Network: finds which missing data matters most and gives farmers small photo and field tasks to fill the gap, with a third reading when two disagree.

- BAS Social & Progression: community, XP, levels and rankings.

- Crop Rotation Engine: explainable rotation options based on climate, soil, crop history and the farmer's own priorities.

What makes Basro different

Photo-diagnosis apps such as Plantix start from a picture of a sick plant. AI advisory chats such as Digital Green's FarmerChat start from a question. Programs such as NASA Harvest bring satellite data to governments and organizations. Basro starts from the farmer's own field and its history, combines NASA data with what the farmer knows, and compares rotation options with their risks and unknowns spelled out. Its community is organized by place and crop, so a farmer learns from neighbors who face the same conditions, and every contribution also improves the field data the advice is built on.

Benefits

Farmers get a clear daily answer instead of a pile of charts, and they can see why. NASA data that is normally hard to find and read becomes useful in the field. Rotation choices are made by comparing options, not by habit, and the farmer stays in charge. Water is used when it is needed. Farmers learn from each other, not only from the app. And because every answer is labeled with its source and its limits, farmers can trust it and know when to ask an expert.

What we hope to achieve

In the long run, we want Basro to become a dataset that follows the world's farmland and soils every day. Farmers build it, farmers use it, and farming gets more efficient. A photo a farmer takes today becomes part of their own field history tomorrow, and with permission it can help another farmer in a similar field. Over time, thousands of farmers' data can form a regional farming memory that, combined with NASA data, helps build better models and gives the ground data that satellite products need to be checked against.

Tools and technologies

- Next.js and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel

- Supabase (PostgreSQL, Storage) for community posts and photos

- Groq vision models, with Google Gemini as fallback

- NASA POWER API, NASA SMAP L4 via NASA AppEEARS, Open-Meteo forecast and seasonal API (ECMWF SEAS5)

- Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the map

- 156 automated tests

- Software: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Supabase, Vercel, Groq, Google Gemini
